steps.observation: Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Key differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid)

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA: Deoxyribose (lacks an –OH group at the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA: Ribose (has an –OH group at the 2′ carbon).  
   Consequence: The extra –OH in RNA makes it more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G).  
   • RNA: Adenine (A), Uracil (U) replaces thymine, Cytosine (C), Guanine (G).

3. Strand architecture  
   • DNA: Typically double-stranded, forming a stable double helix with antiparallel strands (5′→3′ and 3′→5′).  
   • RNA: Usually single-stranded; can fold back on itself to create complex secondary structures (hairpins, loops) and catalytic forms (ribozymes). Some viruses have double-stranded RNA genomes.

4. Molecular size and length  
   • DNA: Very long—complete chromosomes containing millions of base pairs.  
   • RNA: Generally shorter—ranges from ~20 nucleotides (tRNA, miRNA) to thousands (mRNA).

5. Cellular location  
   • DNA: Confined mainly to the nucleus in eukaryotes (and mitochondria/chloroplasts); loose in the cytoplasm of prokaryotes.  
   • RNA: Synthesized in the nucleus (eukaryotes) but functions largely in the cytoplasm; also found in nucleolus, mitochondria, chloroplasts, and, in some viruses, as the genetic material itself.

6. Stability and longevity  
   • DNA: Highly stable; designed for long-term storage of genetic information.  
   • RNA: Relatively unstable and short-lived; suitable for transient roles in gene expression and regulation.

7. Primary biological roles  
   • DNA: Permanent repository of genetic information; template for its own replication and for RNA synthesis (transcription).  
   • RNA: Multiple functional types:  
     – mRNA (messenger): conveys genetic information from DNA to ribosomes.  
     – rRNA (ribosomal): major structural and catalytic component of ribosomes.  
     – tRNA (transfer): brings amino acids to the ribosome during translation.  
     – Regulatory RNAs (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA, etc.): gene expression control.  
     – Catalytic RNAs (ribozymes): enzymatic activity (e.g., self-splicing introns, RNase P).

8. Replication vs. transcription  
   • DNA is replicated (DNA → DNA) during cell division.  
   • RNA is transcribed from DNA (DNA → RNA) and, in special cases like RNA viruses, can be replicated by RNA-dependent RNA polymerases.

9. Repair mechanisms  
   • DNA has extensive proofreading and repair systems to maintain fidelity.  
   • RNA generally lacks such robust repair; errors usually have limited consequences because RNAs are temporary.

10. Helical form  
    • DNA: Predominantly B-form helix (right-handed); can adopt A- or Z-forms under certain conditions.  
    • RNA: When double-stranded, favors the A-form helix due to the 2′-OH group.

Summary  
DNA is the durable, double-stranded, thymine-containing molecule optimized for long-term genetic storage. RNA is the more versatile, single-stranded, uracil-containing molecule specialized for information transfer, regulation, and catalysis, with a generally shorter lifespan and greater chemical reactivity due to its ribose sugar and 2′-OH group.
